name: Judge
label: Revelation
lede: Mike Ferraro quit Youth of Today because he couldn't keep muzzling himself, then wrote Judge's songs so hard the crowds started throwing them back at him. He walked away in 1991 and stayed gone for twenty years.

eras.title: The drummer who quit Youth of Today
eras.text: Mike Ferraro was drumming for Youth of Today and chafing at its non-violent message. He wrote his own songs on the road, quit, named the new band Judge a week later, and asked John "Porcell" Porcelly to help him make it the most militant straight edge band anyone could imagine.

years.src: Vice: Behind the Quiet, Part II
years.h: A broken-down van in Florida ends Ferraro's run in Youth of Today
years.p: Parked at a Florida junkyard on a Youth of Today tour, drummer Mike Ferraro fills a notebook with lyrics that will never fit that band. Back in New York he tells [[Ray Cappo|e8357f9d-f7f5-4858-a766-aef004bb38a6]] he's out.
years.xp:
Ferraro told Vice the pacifist message of Youth of Today clashed with his own violent background, and that he was done holding it in.

A week after quitting he came up with the name Judge and asked Porcell whether he wanted to help.

years.h: Porcell says yes, and Judge gets a guitarist
years.p: Ferraro is sharing a Brooklyn apartment with John "Porcell" Porcelly, Al Brown and Cappo. Porcell pushes him to turn the songs into a real band and signs on to play guitar and bass.

q: I was doing everything to get that reaction.
years.src: Vice: Behind the Quiet, Part II · Wikipedia
years.h: Judge's first record picks a fight with Boston
years.p: [[Mike Ferraro|edffc714-f0a2-4d6c-b4c0-dc31e713481c]] sings and drums, Porcell plays guitar and bass. Five songs, including a cover of Blitz's Warriors, out on Schism, the label Porcell ran with Alex Brown.
years.xp:
Porcell objected that some of Ferraro's first lyrics read like confessions to crimes, and Ferraro rewrote an ending. A reference to Boston on New York Crew still landed as a direct challenge with the crew around the band Choke.

Ferraro says he was chasing exactly that reaction, and was still shocked when it came.

years.big: "Why don't we put a band together and play a show?"
years.src: Vice: Behind the Quiet, Part II
years.h: Judge play the Anthrax in Connecticut with Bold's drummer
years.p: [[Drew Thomas|ebc66701-0d59-49c9-ae21-4937edb96a6a]] of [[Bold|b024b1bd-2020-4b7c-83f7-4660133c89fa]] takes the drums and Jimmy Yu the bass. Yu and drummer [[Luke Abbey|6ab9b327-0f98-4515-907c-13078f426cc5]] become Judge's 1988-89 rhythm section.
years.xp: That's how Ferraro tells it to Vice: the pitch was Porcell's, and the Anthrax was the first room they played. Vice names the drummer only as Drew from Bold.

eras.title: So good they recorded it twice
eras.text: Judge's first album cost real money at Chung King in Manhattan, and the band hated it. They started over in Rhode Island, and Revelation quietly pressed the rejected version for the fans who'd already paid.

years.src: Revelation Records: pressing history · Wikipedia: Bringin' It Down
years.h: Revelation presses the Chung King session Judge rejected
years.p: In January 1989 Judge ran up a real bill recording at Chung King in Manhattan, then threw out the tapes. To cover preorders, Revelation pressed them on white vinyl as Chung King Can Suck It.
years.xp:
The session had Mike Ferraro and Porcell with [[Sammy Siegler|869c662b-574c-46ac-acf6-3dc6f025fd5a]] on drums and Matt Pincus on bass; two of its songs never made Bringin' It Down. Revelation planned 100 copies, but the plant made 110, and the extra ten had the first zero in the hand-numbered /100 written over with a 1.

Jordan Cooper and Porcell both believed only three test pressings existed; Porcell sold one thinking it was a Bringin' It Down test. Copies now sell for over a thousand dollars, and according to Wikipedia one went for $6,600 on eBay. Revelation has said it never made money on them.

years.src: Revelation Records: Judge, Bringin' It Down · Wikipedia: Bringin' It Down
years.h: Bringin' It Down gets a second go in Rhode Island
years.p: Judge re-record at Normandy Sound with Porcell and Tom Soares producing. Revelation's tag line for REV 15: so good they had to record it twice.
years.xp: Normandy Sound is where the [[Cro-Mags|9ffa627f-32c2-4cb1-bfad-00cf348abc70]] cut Best Wishes. Nine songs in 22 minutes.

years.h: Revelation re-presses New York Crew as REV 14
years.p: The debut 7" comes back in an orange sleeve: 4,000 copies on black vinyl and 1,000 on blue.

eras.title: The kids took it literally
eras.text: Judge had set out to provoke, and the provocation worked too well. The last record, There Will Be Quiet..., got darker and more reflective, while the shows filled with fights and worse, and Mike Ferraro decided he couldn't stop what he'd started.

years.h: There Will Be Quiet... slows Judge down
years.p: [[Lars Weiss|c60d8790-7786-4df8-8647-7f8b2ca02c17]] joins on guitar. The Storm and Forget This Time are bleaker than anything on Bringin' It Down; the CD adds a cover of [[Led Zeppelin|678d88b2-87b0-403b-b63d-5da7465aecc3]]'s When the Levee Breaks. REV 20.

years.h: Ex-Judge bassist Jimmy Yu is ordained a Chan Buddhist monk
years.p: Under Master Sheng Yen, Jimmy Yu takes the name Guogu. He later earns a Princeton PhD in 2008 and teaches religion at Florida State University.

years.h: Racist chants and a beating at Judge's Tampa show
years.p: At a Tampa show on the last tour, the Village Voice reported, white power chants start early and a group attacks a Black man in the crowd. Mike Ferraro confronts it from the stage, and Judge ends that year.
years.xp:
From the stage Ferraro asked what six guys on one older man proved, and asked the room to get through the last song in peace. It was a pattern, not one night: at another stop someone called the house Judge were staying in and asked him to go beat up members of the KKK holding a rally in town.

Maximum Rock'N'Roll had long criticized Judge's militant edge, and Ferraro later admitted provocation was the point. He told the Voice the kids were fighting while singing his lyrics at him, and that "I wasn't going to be able to stop what I put in motion years before." So he left.

eras.title: Ferraro goes quiet, the records don't
eras.text: Mike Ferraro left the scene almost completely. Judge's recordings kept circulating, officially and as bootlegs, until Revelation gathered everything onto one disc, What It Meant, in 2005.

years.h: Bootlegs put the rejected Chung King session back out
years.p: No Apologies: The Chung King Sessions and Revelation Can Suck It aren't Revelation releases. A live WNYU broadcast, Vivo En WNYU, circulates alongside them.

years.h: Ferraro goes acoustic as Mike Judge and Old Smoke
years.p: With former Judge roadie Todd Schwartz, he makes a Neil Young-leaning acoustic record, the Sights 12" on Revelation. Then he mostly disappears from music.
years.xp: The disappearance was deliberate. He told the Village Voice: "I just had to walk away for a while, and it just so happened that 'while' turned into something like twenty fucking years."

years.h: A first retrospective lands while Judge sleeps
years.p: What We Said... And Where It Went is Judge's first retrospective.

years.h: Revelation fits all of Judge on one disc
years.p: What It Meant: The Complete Discography arrives sixteen years after Bringin' It Down.

eras.title: Twenty years, then Webster Hall
eras.text: An appearance on East Village Radio drew Mike Ferraro back out after roughly two decades away. The reunion that followed was two nights at Webster Hall in New York, then the world, and a documentary that told the story in the band's own words.

years.h: East Village Radio puts Ferraro back on the air
years.p: He turns up on Black N' Blue Takeover, the appearance that starts Judge's road back.

years.cap: Judge at Alt Stadtbahnhof, Schweinfurt, Germany, May 4, 2014
years.h: Two nights at Webster Hall bring Judge back
years.p: Ferraro, Porcell, [[Sammy Siegler|869c662b-574c-46ac-acf6-3dc6f025fd5a]] and Matt Pincus, with [[Charlie Garriga|4f24f7e7-bc37-45d1-8f60-99bc992cd780]] on second guitar, play New York's Webster Hall. Tours of the US, South America and Europe follow through 2014 and 2015.

years.h: There Will Be Quiet: The Story of Judge (Noisey documentary)
yt: There Will Be Quiet: The Story of Judge (Noisey documentary)

years.h: There Will Be Quiet puts the whole story on film
years.p: Directed by Seth Lowery and Judge drummer Sammy Siegler, the roughly hour-long documentary premieres in four parts through the Village Voice and Noisey.

eras.title: Night one in Los Angeles
eras.text: Judge stayed a working reunion band, the heavy end of the Revelation family on its big bills, with Porcell and Sammy Siegler still behind Mike Ferraro.

years.cap: Judge at Summer Blast, Sala Paral·lel 62, Barcelona, June 23, 2024
years.h: Judge share night one with 7 Seconds in Los Angeles
years.p: Judge co-headline the first of two Book of Revelation Records nights at the 1720. Youth of Today and [[Side By Side|8dc812b1-d387-4c45-8173-f0d5bd0c318f]] take night two.

years.h: Between shows, Ferraro keeps chickens in West Virginia
years.p: According to Wikipedia, the Judge singer raises chickens on a family farm there.
